name: William the Conqueror
role: Duke of Normandy (1035–1087) and King of England (1066–1087)
summary: A medieval ruler who took England by conquest and governed it through personal oaths of loyalty, a new Norman landholding class and close control of the church. Little survives in his own words; his positions appear mainly in acts he ordered, such as the Domesday survey, the harrying of the north, the oath at Salisbury and the laws issued in his name.

property-fundamental.rationale: Mixed record: Law 7 confirms Edward's law over lands and possessions, but he confiscated the lands of Harold's family and of English resisters and transferred them to followers; the Chronicle says his stewards took land 'by right and by unright'.

more-religion-public.rationale: Inferred: the first law attributed to him declares that one God be revered and one faith in Christ kept inviolate throughout his realm; no wider view on public religion is recorded.

gradual-change.rationale: Mixed record: Law 7 keeps King Edward's law and he kept English shires, sheriffs, writs and the danegeld, yet he replaced nearly the whole English ruling class and church leadership within about twenty years.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He claimed the English throne on the strength of Edward the Confessor's alleged promise, was crowned in 1066, held to kingship for the rest of his life and bequeathed the crown to a son.

political-violence-never.rationale: He used war and ravaging to win and hold power, including the winter 1069-70 campaign that laid waste the northern shires; his record shows he held political violence justified.

separate-church-state.rationale: Inferred: he named bishops, convened and shaped church councils with royal and papal legates and issued Law 1 on one faith, which runs against strict separation; he never stated a view on separation.

taxation-theft.rationale: Inferred: he treated taxation as a royal right, continuing the danegeld, imposing 72 pence a hide in 1083 and ordering the Domesday survey to record dues; he never discussed taxation as theft.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He conquered England in 1066 and fought to take Maine (1062-64), invaded Brittany (1064), invaded Scotland (1072) and visited Wales with an army (1081); his reign is a record of expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Law 2 of the laws issued in consultation with his magnates required every freeman to swear loyalty to him, and in 1086 all landholders of account swore oaths of allegiance to him at Sarum; he organised his kingdom as a chain of personal oaths and landholding.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His laws gave Normans a special peace and a murder fine levied on the hundred (Law 3) and set different proof rules for English and French accusers (Law 6).

head-commands-forces.rationale: He personally led his armies, from Hastings to the north campaign, and himself named sheriffs, earls, bishops and deputies; his half-brother and wife governed in his absence at his appointment.

death-penalty.rationale: Law 10 attributed to him forbids killing or hanging for any offence and substitutes blinding and castration, but contested evidence points the other way: the Earl Waltheof was executed in 1076, and the laws' attribution is disputed.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Mixed record: he appointed the Norman bishops and abbots, deposed Stigand and other native prelates, was confirmed in ultimate authority over the Norman church at Lillebonne (1080), raided monastic wealth in 1070 and refused a papal request to do fealty; yet he endowed many monasteries and worked with papal legates.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Inferred: he removed the English aristocracy and installed a new landholding Norman nobility holding heritable fiefs from him; he never spoke to titles as such.

elective-rulers.rationale: Inferred: he fought the nomination of Edgar the Ætheling after Hastings and rested his own claim on designation and conquest, not election; he never addressed election as such.

native-born-offices.rationale: Inferred: he replaced the English holders of earldoms, bishoprics and abbacies with Normans and other continental clergy such as Lanfranc, rather than reserving posts for native English; this reflects his choice of loyal followers, not a stated principle.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He crushed the revolts of 1068-71 and 1075, imprisoned Earl Roger and Odo of Bayeux, and had Waltheof executed; the Chronicle says no man dared act against his will and credits him with a strict peace.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Inferred: Law 1 attributed to him wishes one faith in Christ 'kept ever inviolate' throughout the realm, but it names no penalty for blasphemy or false worship.

dynastic-succession.rationale: On his deathbed he left Normandy to his eldest son Robert and entrusted England to his second son William, expecting him to become king, as reported by later writers.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Mixed record: he issued laws in consultation with his magnates, kept the hundred and shire courts and Edward's law (Laws 7 and 8), but the Chronicle says unlawful exactions grew and 'the more men spake about right law, the more unlawfully they acted'.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He started wars of conquest: the 1066 invasion of England, the conquest of Maine, the Breton campaign and the 1087 raid into the French Vexin in which Mantes was burned.

notes: Sources are chronicles written after or around events (medium at most); the 'Laws of William' text is a collection of articles whose attribution and date are debated. The Harrying of the North's scale is disputed among historians. Pages for the London charter and the Salisbury Oath on Wikipedia do not exist, and the Fordham pages for the Domesday text, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Orderic's deathbed speech returned errors, so those were not used.
